title: 2026 Doomsday Clock Announcement
summary: The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists sets the 2026 Doomsday Clock at its closest ever to midnight, citing nuclear arms racing, an expiring treaty, climate and emerging technology.

assertions.quote: It is now 85 seconds to midnight. This is the closest the world has ever been to midnight.

verdicts.note: The Bulletin set the Clock at 85 seconds to midnight in January 2026, 'the closest it has ever been to catastrophe'.
The 2026 Doomsday Clock statement (27 January 2026) sets the clock at 85 seconds to midnight, closer than 2025's 89 seconds, the previous record.

assertions.quote: will expire, and there is no agreement to replace it.

verdicts.note: The INF and Open Skies treaties ended, Russia suspended New START in 2023, and it expired in February 2026 with no successor.
New START, the last bilateral US-Russia strategic arms treaty, expired in February 2026 with no successor, leaving US and Russian force levels unconstrained.

As of March 2026 US intelligence says Russia undermined arms control, suspended New START data exchanges and deratified the test-ban treaty, but still held to New START's central limits, so the treaties had eroded rather than fully collapsed.

assertions.quote: the potential for a worldwide arms race is upon us.

verdicts.note: XPT superforecasters expected warhead numbers to rise (13,500 by 2040 from 12,705) while nuclear experts expected a fall to 11,990, so forecasters split on a renewed build-up.
The Bulletin judges major-power competition 'a full-blown arms race', citing growing Chinese warheads and platforms and US, Russian and Chinese delivery-system modernization.
SIPRI says the post-Cold War decline in warhead numbers is likely to reverse as dismantlement slows and deployment of new weapons accelerates, with states 'fuelling arms-race dynamics'.
DoD shows China's side of it (heading for 1,000+ warheads by 2030 to achieve 'strategic counterbalance' with the US), but says nothing here about US or Russian build-ups.

US intelligence describes Russia and China modernizing and expanding nuclear forces built to penetrate US missile defences, consistent with intensifying competition, though it does not call it an arms race.

SIPRI says nearly all nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, driven in large part by emerging technologies such as AI, which supports a competitive build-up but does not establish a US-Russia-China arms race as such.

The Bulletin describes growing belligerence among the US, Russia and China in space and a deepening arms race driven by missile defence, with Russia and China contemplating nuclear weapons in space; it shows a strategic arms race, not specifically a race in nuclear arsenals.

assertions.quote: to actually use nuclear weapons on the battlefield, as Russia has threatened to do, as Pakistani officials have threatened to do.

verdicts.note: Russian and Pakistani officials have made such threats, but explicit threats of battlefield use remain confined to a few states.

The Bulletin cites 'lightly veiled Russian nuclear threats' in Ukraine and nuclear brinkmanship in the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, which supports threats being made but does not show a rising trend across nuclear states.
The assessment documents Russian nuclear threats against the US and NATO since 2022 but says nothing of a broader trend among nuclear-armed leaders.

assertions.quote: this could trigger a competition with Russia and China to place their weapons in space

verdicts.note: Russia and China call space interceptors destabilising and are building counterspace weapons, but whether Golden Dome triggers a space arms race is still speculative.

The Bulletin judges that Golden Dome's space-based interceptors raise the probability of conflict in space and are 'likely fueling a new space-based arms race' (an expert judgment, not a measurement).

US intelligence judges that US space-architecture improvements, including plans for hundreds of missile-defence satellites, pose a security dilemma likely to push rivals toward new weapons and more aggressive strategies.

The Bulletin judges that the planned Golden Dome with space-based interceptors will give little real defence but contribute to a deepening, dangerous arms race extending to outer space; an expert assessment.
